unit.unitOverview: Unit 8 is about persuasion: how people share a view and try to bring others with them. You read a school campaign poster, learn to separate a fact that can be proved from an opinion that somebody holds, and take apart the persuasive toolkit of rhetorical questions, emotive language, expert opinion and calls to action. Twenty-five words carry the unit, from evidence and judicial to physiology and hemisphere. Six grammar lessons cover the present perfect with for and since, adverbs of degree with comparatives and superlatives, adjective order, similes, and sequencing words with modal verbs. In the story, Amal and Nora investigate an ancient hall that stands without steps, and prove that a careful question beats a repeated legend.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the four vocabulary groups and learn a few words each day until all twenty-five are secure.
Work through the six grammar lessons one at a time, completing every part of each practice.
Read the garden poster and the toolkit text, then read "The Hall of One Step" in three parts.
Answer the twelve comprehension questions, quoting the passage each one names.
Move through Speaking, Writing and Activities, then take the Share Your Views checkpoint quiz.
Finish with the self-assessment and set one goal for Unit 9.

readings.title: Save Our School Garden!
readings.setting: A school campaign behind the science block
readings.passageScript:
Save Our School Garden!
Dear students, teachers and parents,
Have you ever walked past the empty patch of land behind the science block? Right now it is only dust and stones. Imagine it instead as a green garden full of vegetables, herbs and flowers. We believe our school deserves that garden, and we need your help to build it.
First, a garden teaches skills that last a lifetime. We would learn to plant seeds, water crops and care for living things. Second, growing our own food is healthier and cheaper than buying everything at the market. Fresh tomatoes, onions and herbs could go straight into the school kitchen. Third, a garden would make our school more magnificent than any poster could. Instead of a dusty corner, we would have a central space full of colour and life.
According to a recent study, pupils who work in school gardens score higher marks in science. A physician from the National Health Board has stated that fresh vegetables build stronger bodies and sharper concentration. That is not our opinion; it is evidence.
So what can you do? Every class can donate one bag of soil or one packet of seeds. Teachers, please give us one hour each week for garden time. Parents, if you own tools or know about farming, we would love your help.
A school garden is not merely a pleasant idea. It will teach us teamwork, show us the cycle of growth, and give us a triumph we can all share. Join us at the Garden Launch on Friday at two o'clock, behind the science block.
Written by the Year 5 Garden Committee

readings.title: Fact, Opinion and the Persuasive Toolkit
readings.theme: Fact against opinion, technique and register
readings.passageScript:
Every persuasive text mixes two kinds of sentence, and a careful reader learns to separate them.
A fact can be checked and proved. Consider one claim from the poster: 'A physician studied pupils who eat fresh vegetables.' That is a fact, because you could read the study yourself.
An opinion is what somebody believes or feels. 'The garden is the best idea for our school this year' is an opinion. Another reader might prefer a new library instead.
Whenever you meet persuasive writing, ask yourself one question: can this be proved, or is it simply what somebody thinks?
Writers use a toolkit to move you from thinking to doing. A rhetorical question, such as 'Have you ever walked past that empty patch?', makes you picture the problem rather than answer aloud. Emotive language chooses words like dusty, magnificent and proud, because feelings stay in the memory far longer than numbers. Expert opinion borrows authority from a physician, a geographer or a scientist. Superlative adjectives claim the top place: best, safest, most important. Modal verbs such as should, must and could turn a wish into a duty. Repetition drums one phrase until it sticks, and a call to action tells the reader exactly what to do next.
Register is the final tool, and it depends entirely on the audience. Informal register uses contractions, first person and friendly words, so it suits a note to a classmate. Formal register avoids contractions and keeps a polite distance, so it suits a letter to the headteacher. 'We cannot wait for the garden to open' is formal; 'We can't wait for the garden!' is informal. Choosing the wrong register weakens even the most precise argument.

readings.title: The Hall of One Step, part 1
readings.setting: The highland town of Lomi and its hilltop stone hall
readings.passageScript:
High in the northern highlands, ringed by acacia trees and winding trails, sits a small town called Lomi. It has no airport and no paved roads, but it does have a legend.
“The hall stands without steps,” the people of Lomi say. “No stairs, no ramps — only walls. Yet somehow the builders reached the top.”
Amal's Grade 5 class had heard that legend on every school trip. This time Teacher Yasmin turned the old tale into a proper investigation.
“You will research the stone site,” she said. “Your goal is evidence. Ask questions, use your intelligence, and you may find more than you expect.”
The class split into teams. Amal and Nora formed Team Sandalwood, named after the tree beside the old river path.
As they climbed towards the hall's central courtyard, they passed broken stones and ancient tools. Birds circled above them.
“Too quiet,” said Nora. “It feels like a ceremony that ended before anyone tidied up.”
The hall stood magnificent and tall, its walls covered in symbols and its doors carved with spirals.
“Teacher Yasmin says this hall has stood here for centuries,” said Amal. “And there is honestly no staircase?”
“Not one,” said Nora. “Yet people went inside. That is the whole mystery.”
They circled the building until a low tunnel opened between two rocks.
“This could be the entrance,” Amal said.
“It might also be a trap for goats,” Nora warned.
They crawled through anyway. Inside, the air was cool and every whisper carried a soft echo. The floor was rough, but the walls held hand-painted drawings — evidence of old ideas, stories and planets.
“There is a cycle here,” Nora said, pointing. “Sun, moon, storm, harvest. Then it repeats.”
“That is how early people measured time,” Amal added.

readings.title: The Hall of One Step, part 2
readings.setting: The Grade 5 classroom and the acacia tree outside
readings.passageScript:
At the back of the chamber they found a phrase carved in two languages:
“Power is not in height. One step is a phase.”
Back at school, the teams shared their findings.
“This was never a hall for climbing,” said Nora. “It was built for thinking. Its makers taught that every stage of life is a phase.”
“They linked their ideas to physics and to the stars,” Amal added.
“But how do we know what they thought?” asked Sami.
Amal held up her sketch. “Because they left precise markings. The same marks appear in our history books, copied from old judicial scrolls.”
“Why judicial?” asked Teacher Yasmin.
“Because fair judging was part of how they understood the world,” said Nora. “Citizenship meant knowing the stars, the land and the law.”
Teacher Yasmin smiled. “You have used your minds well, but your work is not finished.”
She held up an envelope. “Inside is a poem written by a physician two hundred years ago. He walked these same hills. Translate it, then present what you learn.”
The team met under the acacia tree the next day, and Nora read the poem aloud.
“I have walked in search of shape,
Wonder a wheel I cannot break.
My heart is not innocent of doubt,
Yet it has stood the physical ache.”
“What does that actually mean?” asked Amal.
“That understanding is never finished,” Nora replied. “It is hard work. It changes, and still it lasts.”
Over the next week the class built a timeline of ideas, connecting philosophy, physics and older stories. They mapped how those ideas travelled across the hemisphere through trade, travel and quiet conversation.
“We have studied for seven days,” Amal said, “and I have never thought this deeply before.”
“I have not worked this hard since last year,” said Nora.
“The spread of these ideas,” Teacher Yasmin added, “was a triumph. Not won by war, but carried by words.”

readings.title: The Hall of One Step, part 3
readings.theme: Presenting ideas and remembering what matters
readings.setting: Presentation day, the hilltop hall and the school roof
readings.passageScript:
The class fell quiet. A light breeze moved through the open windows and the paper timeline fluttered on the wall.
“It is as if the past is still standing beside us,” whispered Amal.
On presentation day the class arranged stones and photographs, words and sketches across three long tables.
Nora explained, “The hall was never about walls. It was about thought. One step was not a staircase; it was a mindset.”
“Our descent into that tunnel was part of the learning,” said Amal. “We climbed down instead of up — down into the story.”
Sami pointed at the map. “Ideas moved like a telegraph, quiet but fast, across towns and across centuries.”
The audience clapped. A visiting geographer from the national museum nodded with real interest.
Afterwards the geographer said, “I have visited many ancient sites, but few pupils have explained the layers so clearly.”
He paused beside one drawing. “This simile — 'the wind in the doorway hummed like a telegraph' — who wrote it?”
“I did,” said Amal, smiling.
“It is quite elegant,” he replied. “Truly expressive.”
That weekend the team hiked back with a flat marker stone, their names written on it in chalk.
“We are not trying to own the hall,” said Amal.
“We are recognising its voice,” added Nora.
They stood quietly. One long ceremony had ended, and a new one had begun.
That evening, sitting on the school roof under the stars, Amal asked, “Do you think we will forget all this?”
“No,” Nora said. “We have seen real things and touched them. You do not forget what feels physical.”
She lay back with her eyes on the sky. “Understanding is not one thing. It is many things held together by wonder.”

grammar.title: The Present Perfect Tense
grammar.explanation: The present perfect ties a past action to the present moment. We build it from have or has plus a past participle. Use it for experiences, achievements and situations that are still going on.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form: subject + have / has + past participle.
Use have with I, you, we and they. Use has with he, she and it.
Regular verbs add -ed: play becomes played, visit becomes visited.
Irregular verbs must be learnt by heart: go becomes gone, see becomes seen, eat becomes eaten, write becomes written.
Examples:
"I have visited the museum."
"He has eaten lunch."
"They have travelled to many countries."
"The hall has stood for centuries."
"She has studied philosophy and physics."
One firm rule: never pair the present perfect with a named past time such as yesterday or last week. Say "I saw him yesterday" for a named time, and "I have seen him before" when no time is given.
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: "He have finished." Fix: "He has finished," because he, she and it always take has.
Mistake: "She has went to the market." Fix: "She has gone to the market," because gone is the past participle.
Mistake: "I have seen him yesterday." Fix: "I saw him yesterday," because a named past time needs the simple past.
grammar.memoryTip: Picture have and has as a bridge. One end rests in the past and the other end reaches into today.
grammar.practice:

Write the present perfect form of the verb in brackets. | They ______ (eat) lunch already. | I ______ (finish) my homework. | She ______ (visit) the zoo three times. | We ______ (see) that film before. | The hall ______ (stand) for centuries. | He ______ (write) a persuasive letter. | Part B. Each sentence holds one error. Rewrite it correctly. | She have finished her homework. | I have went to the market. | He has see the new film. | They has eaten lunch. | We have visited the museum yesterday.

Answer key (self-check): Part A — 1. have eaten 2. have finished 3. has visited 4. have seen 5. has stood 6. has written. Part B — 1. She has finished her homework. 2. I have gone to the market. 3. He has seen the new film. 4. They have eaten lunch. 5. We visited the museum yesterday (a named past time needs the simple past, not the present perfect).

grammar.title: Using "For" and "Since" with the Present Perfect
grammar.explanation: For and since both answer the question how long, but they measure time in different ways. Choosing the right one keeps your timeline precise for your reader.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use for with a length of time.
"I have lived here for five years."
"We have studied English for three months."
"They have known each other for a long time."
Use since with the point where something started.
"I have lived here since 2020."
"She has played football since she was six."
"He has studied geography since last September."
Both words sit inside the present perfect, because the situation began earlier and still continues today.
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: "I have worked here for 2020." Fix: "I have worked here since 2020," because 2020 names a starting point.
Mistake: "I have been happy since two years." Fix: "I have been happy for two years," because two years measures a length.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of for as a ruler that measures how long, and since as a pin stuck in the timeline where the story began.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Write for or since in each gap. | I have supported this team ______ three years. | She has lived in the same town ______ 2021. | We have known each other ______ a very long time. | He has studied geography ______ last September. | They have practised the song ______ two weeks. | Part B. Rewrite each sentence so the time word is correct. | Amal has collected stamps since four years. | Nora has played the drums for she was seven.

Answer key (self-check): Part A — 1. for 2. since 3. for 4. since 5. for. Part B — 1. Amal has collected stamps for four years. 2. Nora has played the drums since she was seven.

grammar.title: Adverbs of Degree, Comparatives and Superlatives
grammar.explanation: Adverbs of degree say how strongly something is true, while comparatives and superlatives rank one thing against others. Together they give a persuasive writer control over the strength of every claim.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Adverbs of degree sit in front of the word they strengthen.
very — "The ceremony was very beautiful."
quite — "He was quite precise in his speech."
really — "The film was really exciting!"
truly — "The ceremony was truly magnificent."
extremely — "She is extremely talented."
Place them before an adjective or another adverb: "He is very tall." "She runs really fast."
Comparatives rank two things. Short adjectives add -er: safer, greener, scarier. Longer adjectives take more: more exciting, more important.
Superlatives rank three or more. Short adjectives add -est: safest, greenest, scariest. Longer adjectives take most: most exciting, most important.
Four common forms are irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst.
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: "He is very unique." Fix: "He is truly unique," because unique already means one of a kind.
Mistake: "This poster is more better." Fix: "This poster is better," because better is already the comparative form.
Mistake: "He is very really nice." Fix: Choose one booster: "He is really nice."
grammar.memoryTip: Treat adverbs of degree as volume dials for adjectives. For ranking, count the syllables: short words take -er and -est, longer words take more and most.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Choose the best adverb of degree from very, quite, really and extremely. | The hall was ______ magnificent. | She is ______ clever for her age. | I am ______ excited about the trip. | The homework was ______ easy. | Part B. Write the comparative and then the superlative form. | good | exciting | scary | bad | important

Answer key (self-check): Part A — these adverbs of degree are close in meaning, so more than one choice can fit correctly in each gap; reasonable model answers are: The hall was very magnificent. She is quite clever for her age. I am really excited about the trip. The homework was extremely easy. Part B — good: better, best. exciting: more exciting, most exciting. scary: scarier, scariest. bad: worse, worst. important: more important, most important.

grammar.title: Adjective Order
grammar.explanation: When two or more adjectives describe one noun, English follows a settled order. Break that order and the phrase still makes sense, but it sounds odd to a reader.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The order runs: quantity, opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.
quantity — one, two, three
opinion — beautiful, interesting, dull
size — big, small, tall
age — old, young, ancient, new
shape — round, square, flat
colour — red, blue, golden
origin — Kenyan, Italian, British
material — wooden, metal, stone
purpose — cooking, sleeping, writing
Examples:
"A beautiful ancient golden statue." (opinion, age, colour)
"A lovely small blue ceramic vase." (opinion, size, colour, material)
"Three exciting new science books." (quantity, opinion, age, purpose)
"An old round wooden table." (age, shape, material)
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: "A golden ancient beautiful statue." Fix: "A beautiful ancient golden statue," so opinion comes before age and colour.
Mistake: "A wooden small brown box." Fix: "A small brown wooden box," so material sits last, next to the noun.
grammar.memoryTip: Say the first letters as one silly word: Q-O-S-A-S-C-O-M-P. Opinion always comes early, and material always sits closest to the noun.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Put the adjectives in their natural order. | I saw a ______ cat. (black, fluffy, small) | She bought a ______ dress. (beautiful, red, long) | They visited a ______ museum. (fascinating, old, local) | We found a ______ stone. (round, ancient, grey) | Part B. One phrase in each pair is correct. Write it out. | a metal large tray or a large metal tray | two Italian old maps or two old Italian maps

Answer key (self-check): Part A — 1. a small fluffy black cat 2. a beautiful long red dress 3. a fascinating old local museum 4. an ancient round grey stone. Part B — 1. a large metal tray 2. two old Italian maps.

grammar.title: Similes
grammar.explanation: A simile compares two unlike things using like or as, so the reader sees your idea instead of merely reading it. The comparison only works when the two things genuinely share a quality.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Build a simile in three steps: pick two different things, decide what they share, then join them with like or as.
Examples:
"The wind in the doorway hummed like a telegraph." (both carry a message over distance)
"Her smile was like sunshine on a rainy day." (both bring sudden warmth)
"The wind howled like a frightened wolf." (both make a loud, wild sound)
"His heart raced like a drum during a parade." (both beat fast and loudly)
The pattern as ... as works the same way: "The night was as dark as a cave."
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: "The car is fast than a rocket." Fix: "The car is as fast as a rocket," because a simile needs like or as, not than.
Mistake: "The cat is like a banana." Fix: Compare things that share a quality, such as "The cat is like a shadow."
grammar.memoryTip: If you can picture the two things side by side and name what they share, the simile works. If you cannot picture it, rewrite it.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Finish each simile with your own idea. | The clouds floated in the sky like ______. | She was as brave as ______. | His laughter rang out like ______. | The old building stood like ______. | Part B. Turn each plain sentence into a simile. | The car was very fast. | The night was dark. | The hall was completely silent.

Self-check (Parts A and B are open-ended — many good similes are possible, so there is no single correct answer): Part A — check that your ending names something that truly shares a quality with the first thing; for example, "The clouds floated in the sky like feathers drifting on the wind" works because both drift gently, "She was as brave as a lion" works because both show fearlessness, "His laughter rang out like a bell" works because both are sudden and clear, and "The old building stood like a watchful giant" works because both feel large and steady. Part B — model similes: "The car was as fast as a rocket." "The night was as dark as a cave." "The hall was as silent as a tomb." Compare your own sentence: does it name two things that share the same quality, joined with like or as?

grammar.title: Linking Words for Sequencing and Modal Verbs
grammar.explanation: Linking words show your reader the order of your reasons, and modal verbs show how strongly you mean them. Persuasive writing needs both: a clear route through the argument and a clear level of urgency.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Sequencing words signpost the argument.
First / Firstly — open the first point.
Next / Then / After that — carry the sequence on.
In addition / Furthermore / Moreover — add weight to a point.
Finally / Lastly / In conclusion — close the argument.
Modal verbs set the strength of a claim.
must — strongest: "Every school must protect its garden."
should — firm advice: "Teachers should give us one hour each week."
could — a possibility: "We could plant herbs beside the wall."
might — the weakest: "Parents might lend us some tools."
Examples from the story: "First, they gathered." "Then, the ceremony began." "Finally, they celebrated the triumph."
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: Writing "Finally" before "First", so the reader loses the thread. Fix: Plan the order before you draft, then signpost it.
Mistake: "You must maybe join us." Fix: Choose one strength: "You must join us," or "You might join us."
grammar.memoryTip: First, Next, Finally maps the beginning, middle and end of any argument. For modals, picture a dial: might, could, should, must.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Fill each gap with First, Then or Finally. | ______, we gathered our research materials. | ______, we analysed the evidence carefully. | ______, we presented our findings to the class. | Part B. Choose must, should, could or might for each gap. | Every pupil ______ wear a coat outdoors in the rain. | The school ______ plant herbs beside the kitchen door. | Parents ______ lend us tools if they have any spare. | Teachers ______ give us one hour a week, because the garden needs care. | Part C. Add a linking word that adds weight to the point. | A garden teaches teamwork. ______, it saves the school money.

Answer key (self-check): Part A — 1. First 2. Then 3. Finally. Part B — 1. must 2. could 3. might 4. should. Part C — In addition / Furthermore / Moreover, it saves the school money (any of these three linking words works).

writing.title: Writing 1: Plan a Persuasive Argument
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Plan a persuasive piece before you write a single full sentence.
Choose your subject, then fill four boxes.
Box 1, introduction: state your view in one sentence and hook the reader.
Box 2, reasons: list three reasons and note the fact or example that supports each one.
Box 3, counter-argument: write what somebody who disagrees would say, and your answer to them.
Box 4, conclusion: repeat your view in fresh words and finish with a call to action.
Bring the completed plan to your next teacher session.
writing.modelText:
Box 1, introduction: I believe that our school needs a shaded reading corner. Have you ever tried to read in the midday sun?
Box 2, reasons: reading every day builds vocabulary (fact: our recent class test showed daily readers scored higher); shade protects books (the library's magnificent atlas has faded brown); a quiet corner helps younger pupils (Grade 1 read outside during exams).
Box 3, counter-argument: some might say the money should buy footballs, but a corner costs less than one term of new balls and lasts for years.
Box 4, conclusion: a reading corner is a decent, cheap gift to every pupil, so let us ask the headteacher this Friday.
writing.expectedLength: One planning grid of four boxes

items: Box 1, introduction: I believe our school should start a recycling programme. Have you ever noticed how much paper we throw away in one week?

Box 2, reasons: recycling paper saves trees (fact: one recycled tonne of paper saves roughly seventeen trees); it teaches responsibility (example: the Grade 6 eco club already sorts bottles); it can raise money for school trips (example: some schools sell scrap paper to local traders).
Box 3, counter-argument: some might say sorting rubbish wastes lesson time, but two labelled bins by the canteen would take seconds to use and cost almost nothing.
Box 4, conclusion: a recycling programme is a small change with a lasting benefit, so let us ask the headteacher to trial it for one term.
otherAnswers: Any genuine subject your school needs works just as well, such as more library books or longer breaks for younger pupils, as long as each box still holds real reasons and a genuine counter-argument.
The call to action can be different too, such as asking to meet the school council instead of the headteacher directly.

writing.successCriteria: I stated one clear view; I gave three reasons with evidence; I answered a counter-argument; I ended with a call to action
writing.support: Talk each box through aloud before writing, and borrow the structure of the school garden poster.
writing.extension: Rank your three reasons from weakest to strongest, then plan to finish on the strongest one.

writing.title: Writing 2: A Persuasive Poster
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Design a poster that persuades pupils to do one useful thing.
Choose from joining a reading club, taking part in a clean-up day, eating healthier lunches or helping younger pupils.
Your poster needs a bold title, at least two reasons, and one rhetorical question that makes the reader stop.
Use at least one comparative or superlative adjective, and one modal verb.
Finish with a call to action that names what to do, when to do it and where to go.
Keep the words few and the layout clear, because a poster is read while walking past.
writing.modelText:
Join the Clean-Up Day!
Have you ever wondered why the path behind the science block is the dirtiest place in school? Rubbish makes our playground uglier than any other in Lomi, and it can hurt the birds that nest in the acacia trees. Together we can make ours the cleanest school in the highlands. You should bring gloves and a bin bag to the main gate at 8 o'clock on Saturday.
writing.expectedLength: One poster of roughly sixty words

items: Title: Choose the Better Lunch!
Rhetorical question: Have you ever felt sleepy after a lunch of chips and sweets?
Reason 1: Fruit and vegetables give you more energy than fried food for the whole afternoon.
Reason 2: A healthier lunch is the cheapest way to keep your body strong and your mind sharp.
Comparative, superlative and modal verb: You should always choose the freshest option in the canteen.
Call to action: Pick one fruit and one vegetable at lunch, starting this Monday, at the canteen counter.
otherAnswers: The poster could instead promote joining the reading club, taking part in a clean-up day, or helping younger pupils, as long as it still has a bold title, two reasons, a rhetorical question, a comparative or superlative adjective, a modal verb and a clear call to action.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote a bold title; I gave two reasons; I asked a rhetorical question; I used a comparative or superlative; I ended with a clear call to action
writing.support: Sketch the layout in pencil first and write the slogan last, once the reasons are settled.
writing.extension: Write a second version of the slogan for a younger audience, and explain which one works better.

writing.title: Writing 3: A Formal Letter to the Headteacher
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a formal letter asking the headteacher for something your school genuinely needs.
It could be a reading corner, more sports equipment or a garden.
Set out your address and the date at the top right, then open with Dear followed by the headteacher's name.
Paragraph one says what you are writing about and what you want.
Paragraph two gives two or three reasons supported by facts.
Paragraph three says exactly what you would like the headteacher to do next.
Sign off with Yours sincerely and your full name, and use no contractions anywhere in the letter.
writing.modelText:
14 Acacia Road, Lomi
3 May 2026
Dear Mrs Farah,
I am writing to request a school garden on the empty patch behind the science block.
A garden would teach us to grow food, which is a skill for life. Fresh vegetables are also healthier and cheaper than food bought at the market, and a physician's recent study showed that pupils who eat them concentrate better. Our class has already collected forty signatures.
We would be grateful if you could visit the site with us next Monday and approve a small starting budget.
Yours sincerely,
Amal Hassan
writing.expectedLength: Three paragraphs plus greeting and sign-off

items: Address and date: 22 Baobab Street, Lomi — 5 May 2026
Greeting: Dear Mr Ali,
Paragraph 1: I am writing to request more sports equipment for our lunchtime games, in particular new footballs and skipping ropes.

Paragraph 2: Regular exercise helps pupils concentrate in class, and a survey by our own class found that most pupils have nothing to play with at break. The current equipment is over three years old, and several balls are punctured.
Paragraph 3: We would be grateful if you could consider ordering new equipment before the start of next term.
Sign-off: Yours sincerely, Idris Warsame
otherAnswers: Any genuine school need works instead, such as a reading corner or a garden, as long as the address-and-date layout, three paragraphs, formal tone and sign-off all stay the same.

writing.successCriteria: I used the formal layout; I stated my request clearly; I gave reasons with facts; I avoided every contraction; I said what should happen next
writing.support: Draft the letter informally first, then rewrite each contraction as two full words.
writing.extension: Add one sentence that acknowledges the cost of your request and explains why it is still worth it.

writing.title: Writing 4: A Film or Book Review
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Review a film you have watched or a book you have read this term.
Name the title, the genre and the director or author in your first sentence.
Summarise the plot in two or three sentences, and give away no endings.
Share your opinion honestly: say what you liked and what could have been better.
Use comparative adjectives to measure it against another film or book you know.
Close with a rating out of five stars and a recommendation that names the right reader.
writing.modelText: A useful review separates plot from judgement. Every judgement carries a reason, such as "The ending felt rushed, because two characters vanish."
writing.sentenceStarter: If you enjoy ..., you should read ...

items: Paragraph 1: The Clockwork Falcon is an adventure film directed by Mariam Osei. It follows a young mechanic named Deka, who repairs an old flying machine after her village loses its only working generator. When the machine turns out to hold a secret stranger than anyone expected, Deka must decide who she can trust before the neighbouring town finds out what she has discovered.

Paragraph 2: I liked how patiently the film builds Deka's confidence, though the middle section felt slower than the exciting opening ten minutes. It is more thoughtful than most adventure films I have watched, which usually rush straight into the action. I would give it four stars out of five, and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys a quiet hero more than a loud one.
otherAnswers: Any film watched or book read this term works just as well, as long as the review names the title, genre and author or director in the first sentence, summarises without spoilers, gives reasoned opinions, uses a comparative adjective, and ends with a rating and a recommendation.

writing.successCriteria: I named the title, genre and author; I summarised without spoilers; I gave reasons for my opinion; I used a comparative adjective; I gave a rating and a recommendation
writing.support: List three things you liked and three you did not before you begin the paragraphs.
writing.extension: Rewrite your closing recommendation for a reader who disliked the genre, and see whether it still persuades.

writing.title: Writing 5: A Reflection on the Hall of One Step
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short reflection of five sentences about what the story taught you.
Use the present perfect at least twice, for example "I have learnt that evidence matters more than a legend".
Name one moment in the story that changed your thinking, and quote three or four words from the passage.
Explain what you would do differently if your class investigated an old site.
Finish with one question the story left unanswered for you.
writing.modelText: A reflection is not a retelling. Two sentences on what happened is plenty; the other three should explain what it changed in you.

items: I have learnt that a legend is only the beginning of a story, never the end of it.
The moment that changed my thinking was when Nora read the carved phrase, "One step is a phase," because I had always believed that power came from height rather than from an idea.
I have never thought as carefully about evidence as I did while watching Amal and Nora test every guess before they trusted it.
If my class investigated an old site, I would photograph every marking before anyone touched it, so that no clue was lost by accident.
Did the physician who wrote the poem ever find the shape he was searching for, or does his search continue even now?

writing.successCriteria: I used the present perfect twice; I quoted from the passage; I explained what changed my thinking; I ended with a real question
writing.support: Underline three phrases in the story that struck you, and build a sentence around each.
writing.extension: Rewrite your last sentence as a rhetorical question and decide which version is stronger.

writing.title: Writing 6: A Four-Line Poem with a Simile
writing.promptAndInstructions:
The physician in the story left a four-line poem about wonder and doubt.
Write your own four-line poem about something you believe matters, such as fairness, curiosity or friendship.
Include one simile that uses like or as, and make sure the two things you compare truly share a quality.
Read the poem aloud twice, once for meaning and once for rhythm, and change any word that trips your tongue.
Write one sentence underneath explaining what your simile is doing.
writing.modelText: Aim for one strong image rather than four weak ones, and let the last line answer or unsettle the first.
writing.expectedLength: Four lines plus one sentence of explanation

items: Line 1: Curiosity is like a torch in a quiet cave,
Line 2: It shows one step, then asks for one step more.
Line 3: It never waits for courage to arrive first,
Line 4: It simply walks until it finds the door.
Explanation: My simile compares curiosity to a torch because neither one shows everything at once, yet each lights up just enough of the next step to keep you moving forward.
otherAnswers: The poem could focus on fairness or friendship instead, or on any other quality you believe truly matters, as long as it still uses a simile that compares two things that share a real quality.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote exactly four lines; I included one simile; the comparison shares a real quality; I explained what my simile does
writing.support: Start from the simile and build the other three lines around it.
writing.extension: Write a second version that replaces the simile with a metaphor, then compare the effect.

Use at least five words from this unit and underline each one as you go.
Use the present perfect at least once, for example "I have never seen anything like it".
Read the paragraph aloud to an adult if one is nearby, or read it aloud to yourself, then change one word for a more precise one.
Write the word you replaced and the word you chose at the bottom of the page.

assignments.title: Share Your Views learning portfolio
assignments.instructions:
Submit three pieces: the formal letter from Writing 3, the persuasive poster from Writing 2, and a recording of the one-minute speech from Speaking 1.
Marking guidance for the teacher. Award the writing marks against the four writing criteria, giving credit for a clear view, three reasons with evidence, an answered counter-argument and a call to action. The letter must contain no contractions; deduct nothing for a single slip, but note it for redrafting. Award the speaking marks against the four speaking criteria, listening for evidence attached to each reason and for a closing call to action. The full mark is thirty-two, split sixteen for writing and sixteen for speaking.
Redraft each piece once using the rubric before you submit it.

quizzes.question: Which sentence from the school garden poster is a fact rather than an opinion?
quizzes.options: The patch of land sits behind the science block. | A garden would make our school more magnificent. | The garden is the best idea for our school this year. | Gardening is far more enjoyable than reading indoors.
quizzes.correctAnswer: The patch of land sits behind the science block.
quizzes.explanation: Only the first statement can be checked by walking outside; the other three describe what somebody feels.

quizzes.question: Which word names the study of how living bodies work?
quizzes.explanation: Physiology studies how bodies function; a telegraph sends messages, a ceremony marks an event and a descent is a way down.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses the present perfect correctly?
quizzes.options: She have finished her poster. | She has finished her poster. | She has finish her poster. | She have finish her poster.
quizzes.explanation: She takes has, and the verb must be the past participle finished, so only the second option is correct.

quizzes.question: Complete the sentence: Amal has lived in Lomi ______ 2021.
quizzes.explanation: The year 2021 names the starting point of the situation, and a starting point always takes since.

quizzes.question: Which phrase places the adjectives in the natural English order?
quizzes.options: a grey round ancient stone | an ancient round grey stone | a round ancient grey stone | an ancient grey round stone
quizzes.explanation: English orders adjectives by age, then shape, then colour, which gives ancient, round, grey.

quizzes.question: Which line from the story is a simile?
quizzes.options: Ideas moved like a telegraph, quiet but fast. | The hall stood magnificent and tall. | Amal held up her sketch. | Birds circled above them.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Ideas moved like a telegraph, quiet but fast.
quizzes.explanation: A simile compares two unlike things with like or as, and only the first line makes that comparison.

quizzes.question: In The Hall of One Step, what does the carved phrase say about power?
quizzes.options: Power belongs to the tallest building. | Power grows out of wealth and trade. | Power is not in height; one step is a phase. | Power is measured by counting the steps.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Power is not in height; one step is a phase.
quizzes.explanation: The carving separates power from height entirely, which is why Nora reads the hall as a place built for thinking.

quizzes.question: Which modal verb makes the strongest recommendation in a persuasive letter?
quizzes.explanation: Must states an obligation, while might, could and may only offer a possibility.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses formal register for a letter to the headteacher?
quizzes.options: We can't wait for the garden to be ready! | I am writing to request a garden behind the science block. | You guys should totally come along on Friday. | It's gonna be the best thing our school has ever done.
quizzes.correctAnswer: I am writing to request a garden behind the science block.
quizzes.explanation: Formal register avoids contractions and slang, so only the second option suits a letter to a headteacher.

quizzes.question: Which word means exact and accurate rather than vague?
quizzes.explanation: Precise describes exact detail; innocent means not guilty, scarce means hard to find and decent means merely good enough.

teacherNotes.note: Pre-teach the four phys- words together, because learners meet physics, physical, physician and physiology in the same fortnight and reliably confuse them. Model the decent and descent pair aloud on day one. The story turns a local legend into an investigation, so keep the emphasis on evidence rather than on belief, and welcome learners who arrive with different family traditions. An adult must sit with the learner for every AI tutor task, every debate and every recording; a child is never left alone with the device, and recordings stay inside the class space. Give feedback on complete sentences, on the past participle in present perfect answers, and on whether each persuasive claim carried evidence.

teacherNotes.noteType: Grammar answer key and tutor guidance
teacherNotes.note:
Grammar answers, teacher copy. Grammar 1 Part A: have eaten, have finished, has visited, have seen, has stood, has written. Part B: She has finished her homework. I have gone to the market. He has seen the new film. They have eaten lunch. We visited the museum yesterday. Grammar 2 Part A: for, since, for, since, for. Part B: Amal has collected stamps for four years. Nora has played the drums since she was seven. Grammar 3 Part A, suggested: truly or really, quite, really, extremely or quite. Part B: better and best; more exciting and most exciting; scarier and scariest; worse and worst; more important and most important. Grammar 4 Part A: a small fluffy black cat; a beautiful long red dress; a fascinating old local museum; an ancient round grey stone. Part B: a large metal tray; two old Italian maps. Grammar 5: answers vary, so check that like or as appears and that the two things share a real quality. Grammar 6 Part A: First, Then, Finally. Part B: must, could, might, should. Part C: In addition, Furthermore or Moreover.
Tutor guidance. The most useful requests are asking the tutor to contrast physiology with physics, to explain descent against decent, to act as a debate partner on the school garden, and to check whether every reason in a speech carried evidence. Every one of these requests is made with an adult sitting alongside.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Rhetorical question: "Have you ever walked past the empty patch of land behind the science block?" Fact: the physician from the National Health Board. Opinion: "a garden would make our school more magnificent". Modal verb: would, could or can. Comparative: "more magnificent than any poster could". Call to action: "Join us at the Garden Launch on Friday at two o'clock." Mark the effect column, not the quotation.

1 F, 2 O, 3 F, 4 O, 5 F, 6 O. Item 3 is the one learners most often mislabel: it reports a study, so it can be checked even though it sounds like praise. Award the second mark only when the learner says how the statement could be proved.

Suggested rewrites: 1 We are eager for the garden to be ready. 2 We encourage every pupil to attend the event. 3 It will be an outstanding occasion. 4 I believe the library requires more books. Accept any version with no contraction and no slang; the underlined word should be the formal choice, such as encourage, require or occasion.

Part A: 1 evidence, 2 persuasive, 3 physician, 4 triumph, 5 promote. Part B: 1 cycle, 2 evidence, 3 judicial, 4 physician, 5 ancient. Watch for descent chosen instead of evidence in Part B item 2, and ask that learner to say both words aloud.

Part A: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b, 5-e. Part B: physics, physical, physician and physiology all come from the Greek root phys, meaning nature or body. Philosophy is the odd one out, from philo meaning love and sophia meaning wisdom.

Mark the underlining first: five unit words must be visible. Then check for one present perfect verb, and finally the recorded word swap at the foot of the page. A paragraph with five words but no upgrade is not yet complete.
Correct: the patch of land sits behind the science block. It is the only statement a reader could verify by looking. Learners who choose the magnificent option are hearing praise as proof.
Correct: physiology. Point learners to the shared root phys, then contrast it with telegraph, ceremony and descent, none of which name a field of study.
Correct: she has finished her poster. Check both halves of the answer, because many learners fix the auxiliary and leave the base verb finish in place.
Correct: since. Ask the learner to say whether 2021 is a length of time or a starting point; naming it as a starting point secures the rule.
Correct: an ancient round grey stone. Have the learner label each adjective as age, shape or colour before checking the order.
Correct: ideas moved like a telegraph, quiet but fast. The word like is the signal, and the two things compared genuinely share speed and quietness.
Correct: power is not in height; one step is a phase. Learners who choose the counting option are reading the word step literally rather than as a stage of life.
Correct: must. Rank all four modals aloud from weakest to strongest, so the learner hears might, could, may and then must.
Correct: I am writing to request a garden behind the science block. The other three all carry a contraction or slang, which no formal letter should hold.
Correct: precise. Ask for a one-word gloss of each distractor, because innocent, scarce and decent are all Unit 8 words with quite different meanings.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Share Your Views" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 9-10 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'intelligence'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Read persuasive posters, information texts and narrative, and identify how each one presents a viewpoint.
Distinguish a fact that can be proved from an opinion that somebody merely holds.
Use adverbs of degree, comparative adjectives and superlative adjectives to strengthen a claim.
Choose formal or informal register to match the audience of a letter, a poster or a debate.
Use the present perfect, with for and since, to link past experience to the present.
Use modal verbs such as must, should, could and might to grade the strength of an opinion.
Plan and write a persuasive poster, a formal letter and a review, using figurative language where it helps.
Present a view aloud with evidence, and respond to a listener who disagrees.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "Save Our School Garden!" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Hall of One Step, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "The Present Perfect Tense" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. These are the signs the unit has landed — listen for them in conversation and look for them in the writing:

The formal letter written without contractions, plus the four rewritten sentences in Activity 3.
Grammar 1 and 2 practice, plus two present perfect verbs in the story reflection.
Grammar 6 Part B, and one modal verb used in every debate turn.
The four-box plan, the finished poster, the letter, the review and the four-line simile poem.
The recorded one-minute speech, the paired debate and the question time on the story.
